TRADE SECRET MISAPPROPRIATION CEASE AND DESIST LETTER
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS LETTER
This letter is sent by Acme, Inc. to Jordan Lee concerning trade secret information that Acme, Inc. owns or controls. Acme, Inc. is sending this letter to describe its concerns and to request specific actions in response, by no later than September 15, 2026.

DESCRIPTION OF THE TRADE SECRET AND THE CONDUCT AT ISSUE
Acme, Inc. identifies the trade secret information at issue as follows: Acme's proprietary customer-pricing algorithm and associated source code

Based on information currently available to Acme, Inc., the following describes conduct that Acme, Inc. believes may involve the acquisition, disclosure, or use of that information without Acme, Inc.'s consent: Recipient appears to have retained and used Acme's pricing algorithm files after leaving Acme's employment

This description reflects Acme, Inc.'s current understanding. It is not a judicial finding, and nothing in this letter states that a court has determined that misappropriation occurred.

FEDERAL CIVIL CAUSE OF ACTION FOR TRADE SECRET MISAPPROPRIATION
Federal law gives the owner of a trade secret a private civil cause of action for misappropriation, but only where the trade secret is related to a product or service used in, or intended for use in, interstate or foreign commerce. A civil action under this federal law generally must be brought within three years after the misappropriation is discovered, or after it should have been discovered through reasonable diligence; a misappropriation that continues over time counts as a single claim for this purpose, not a separate claim each time it recurs.

  — 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, private civil action (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1836)
  "A civil action under subsection (b) may not be commenced later than 3 years after the date on which the misappropriation with respect to which the action would relate is discovered or by the exercise of reasonable diligence should have been discovered. For purposes of this subsection, a continuing misappropriation constitutes a single claim of misappropriation."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1836(d) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, period of limitations (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1836)

FEDERAL DEFINITION OF "MISAPPROPRIATION" AND "IMPROPER MEANS"
Federal law defines "misappropriation" of a trade secret to cover two distinct situations: acquiring a trade secret while knowing or having reason to know it was acquired by improper means, and disclosing or using a trade secret without consent under specified circumstances — including where the person used improper means to acquire it, or knew or had reason to know they owed a duty to keep it secret or limit its use. "Improper means" is itself a separately defined term; it includes theft, bribery, misrepresentation, breach or inducement of breach of a duty to maintain secrecy, and espionage, but it specifically excludes reverse engineering, independent derivation, and other lawful means of acquiring the same information.

  "the term "misappropriation" means— (A) acquisition of a trade secret of another by a person who knows or has reason to know that the trade secret was acquired by improper means; or (B) disclosure or use of a trade secret of another without express or implied consent by a person who— (i) used improper means to acquire knowledge of the trade secret; (ii) at the time of disclosure or use, knew or had reason to know that the knowledge of the trade secret was— (I) derived from or through a person who had used improper means to acquire the trade secret; (II) acquired under circumstances giving rise to a duty to maintain the secrecy of the trade secret or limit the use of the trade secret; or (III) derived from or through a person who owed a duty to the person seeking relief to maintain the secrecy of the trade secret or limit the use of the trade secret; or (iii) before a material change of the position of the person, knew or had reason to know that— (I) the trade secret was a trade secret; and (II) knowledge of the trade secret had been acquired by accident or mistake"
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1839(5) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, definition of "misappropriation" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1839)

  — 18 U.S.C. § 1839(6) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, definition of "improper means" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1839)

FEDERAL CIVIL REMEDIES FOR TRADE SECRET MISAPPROPRIATION
In a federal civil action for trade secret misappropriation, a court may grant injunctive relief; award damages for the trade secret owner's actual loss and for the misappropriator's unjust enrichment not already captured in that loss figure, or, in place of those damages, impose a reasonable royalty for the unauthorized disclosure or use; and, where the trade secret was willfully and maliciously misappropriated, award exemplary damages of up to two times the damages awarded, plus reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party. Federal law separately authorizes an extraordinary, ex parte civil seizure remedy in limited circumstances; that seizure remedy is a different provision and isn't addressed by this clause.

CALIFORNIA'S DEFINITION OF MISAPPROPRIATION
California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act separately defines "misappropriation." Under that statute, misappropriation includes acquiring a trade secret while knowing or having reason to know it was acquired by improper means, and it also includes disclosing or using a trade secret without express or implied consent under specified circumstances — including where the person used improper means to acquire it, or knew or had reason to know they owed a duty to keep it secret or limit its use. This definition is substantively similar to the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act's own misappropriation definition, though the two statutes use some different phrasing, and both a federal DTSA claim and a California UTSA claim can potentially be based on the same underlying conduct.

CALIFORNIA'S REMEDIES FOR TRADE SECRET MISAPPROPRIATION
California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act allows a complainant to recover damages for actual loss caused by misappropriation, plus damages for unjust enrichment caused by the misappropriation that isn't already counted in the actual-loss figure. If neither actual loss nor unjust enrichment can be proven, the statute instead allows a court to order payment of a reasonable royalty for no longer than the period the use could have been prohibited. REQUESTED ACTIONS AND RESPONSE DEADLINE

Acme, Inc. requests a written response by that date.
